entry.title: Tiny model, full provenance — where Apache Sourcelume is, and where it is heading
entry.summary: Apache Sourcelume now records provenance for models as well as datasets, and a sample project trains a tiny model that writes its own training provenance record as part of the run.
entry.content:
Ask anyone who ships a language model a simple question: which data was this trained on, and what license comes with it? The honest answer today is a shrug with a bibliography. Training corpora are assembled from dozens or hundreds of sources, licensing information is missing, wrong, or unverifiable — a 2024 audit found license-omission rates above 70% across popular dataset-hosting sites — and what a producer does publish is usually a claim you have to take on faith: a paragraph in a paper, a model card, a PDF. Nothing you can check.

What Sourcelume is

That is the gap Apache Sourcelume is built for. It is not a certification authority and it does not decide whether anyone's licensing claims are true. It is plumbing: a versioned, JSON-LD metadata specification for dataset origin, custody chain, and licensing; a reference registry built on Apache Atlas that stores and serves those records through plain REST APIs; and tooling that turns "documenting your data" from a favor into a build step. The point is narrower and more radical than a licensing database: when a claim is published as a record, in a shared shape, at a stable identifier, then others can finally check it — resolve it, compare it, count it — instead of trusting it.

Datasets, and then models

The dataset side of this is already real. The spec's ProvenanceRecord has been exercised against a public example we could find: the DFM Mímir training corpus. We verified dataset by dataset, straight from the report's own tables. But records about datasets were only ever half of the question.

On the model side, the situation is inverted: model producers know exactly what they trained on, but there has been no neutral place to say it. When a downstream consumer recently asked whether they could fetch structured provenance for a model — machine-readable, not prose — the piece that would answer them did not exist. The mental model that emerged in the discussion was an SBOM for models: software bills of materials let a shipped artifact declare its ingredients; a model should be able to do the same for its training data, with the producer attesting to the list. So Sourcelume grew a second record type: the TrainingProvenanceRecord. A model producer publishes it; it references dataset records by their canonical identifiers, with token counts and shares; it can say disclosure: complete, partial, or honestly undisclosed, because an honest "we don't disclose" is also information worth publishing.

A record you can watch being born

Which brings us to the demo, because a record type is only as real as a record you can watch being born. The apache/sourcelume-sample repository trains a character-level language model of 71,891 parameters, on a corpus every reader knows is public domain: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Project Gutenberg ebook #11, 1865. Then, in the same run, the trainer writes the model's provenance record: a TrainingProvenanceRecord pointing at the dataset record by its canonical IRI, with the actual numbers from the run — tokens, share, loss, timestamp.

This is where the sober result lands. Not a claim restated in a PDF paper — the run's own tokens, shares, and loss now sit in Sourcelume, written by the trainer that produced them. And as the sample shows, the whole thing drops straight into existing build tooling. Nothing is reconstructed by hand after the fact: the record is written where the data is already being used, in the same pipeline that trains the model.

Our sample code lives at github.com/apache/sourcelume-sample for those who would like to dive in.

What it does not do yet

As it stands today, Sourcelume can show the data that was deposited in it. What it does not do yet — and where community discussion still needs to happen — is verify that any of it is true. Today, Sourcelume's job is exactly this: information can be filed and fetched back by machines. Our community is working towards its initial release goals, with attestation features becoming our next target.

Getting involved

Sourcelume is an open project, and there is room to help shape what comes next. Whether you're interested in provenance metadata, dataset licensing, model training, API design, or responsible AI more broadly, we welcome people who want to help build and test the specification, contribute to the reference implementation, improve the examples and documentation, or participate in discussions about how provenance claims should be represented and eventually verified.

If this work interests you, join the Apache Sourcelume community. Explore the code and examples, try the sample training pipeline, share your feedback, or get involved in the discussions around the project's next milestones. The goal is not just to make provenance machine-readable, but to build an open, community-driven infrastructure that makes it easier to understand where datasets and models come from — and what we can actually verify about them.

Apache Sourcelume is an ASF Top-level Project. For more information, visit sourcelume.apache.org.

Achim Nierbeck is an ASF Member and a member of the Apache Karaf and Apache Sourcelume PMCs. Jamie Goodyear is an ASF Member and Vice President, Apache Sourcelume.

entry.title: Responsible AI at Community Over Code, Glasgow
entry.summary: The Responsible AI initiative brought two sessions and a hackathon slot to Community Over Code in Glasgow. This included a working session on llm.apache.org and a roundtable on what AI is doing to open source maintainership.
entry.content:
Community Over Code ran from 11 to 14 October at the Hilton Glasgow, and the Responsible AI (RAI) Initiative was there with two sessions on the Monday and a slot in the hackathon room alongside them. This is a short account of what we did, what we heard, and what happens next.

The hackathon: getting people onto llm.apache.org

The RAI hackathon session was built around one practical goal: get committers signed in to llm.apache.org and making their first model call before they left the room.

LLMAO is the Foundation's LLM gateway. It exists because the alternative of every project signing up for its own provider account and holding its own keys, scales badly and leaves the Foundation with no way to see what is being spent, on whose behalf, or against which model. The gateway gives the ASF a single sanctioned path to inference: you authenticate with your Apache identity, you get a credential scoped to a project, and the usage is attributed to that project and to you. Projects do not need their own vendor relationship to get useful work done, and the Foundation can answer for the cost and the policy in one place.

For anyone who did not make it to Glasgow, the sign-up path is the same one we walked through in the room, and the gateway is OpenAI-compatible. In most cases pointing an existing client at a new base URL and key is the whole integration.

The hackathon ran Monday through Wednesday in the Wee Dram Room, with projects claiming half-day slots across the three days. Responsible AI shared the schedule with ASF Tooling, Apache Magpie, Apache Sourcelume, Apache Search and a long list of others. See the hackathon page for how the time was carved up.

The Roundtable: What AI is Doing to Maintainership

The Responsible AI Roundtable put six people on a panel — David Fisher, Holden Karau, Andrew Musselman, Jarek Potiuk, Tim Storer, and Jeff Genender, VP RAI — and opened the floor.

The questions on the table were the uncomfortable ones rather than the promotional ones:

  • How do you attract and keep committers when automated shortcuts are available for the work that used to be how people earned their way in?
  • What does meritocracy mean under the Apache Way when a contribution's provenance is harder to read than it used to be?
  • How do you re-engage maintainers staring down a large legacy refactor that a model could attempt but not be accountable for?
  • What do projects do about the rising volume of automated vulnerability reports and low-quality submissions, which cost real maintainer attention whether or not they are valid?
  • Underneath all of it: What is the risk to open source innovation if the answer to each of these is handled badly?

There was lively discussion, with perspectives covering the individual maintainer, project committee manager, tooling and platform owners, and a welcome academic view. Thought-provoking questions from the audience included how to include and mentor junior engineers in an environment where everyone has a "head start" already with their tools, what the shape of contributions will take in the future, how incentives will change over time, and what motivates software engineers at their core.

Where the platform actually is

The sessions were grounded in work that already exists rather than a roadmap, so it is worth saying plainly what runs today and what does not.

LLMAO is the gateway described above: metered, attributed model access for Apache projects, at llm.apache.org.

Gofannon is an agent workbench for the Foundation, based on the project of the same name that originated at the AI Alliance. It is where agents get built and run, so that a project can get useful work done without standing up its own infrastructure.

Memory is the newest piece, and the least built. The problem it addresses is that agents start every run empty: a scan run this month has no idea what last month's scan found or what the project already fixed. Memory gives agents somewhere to write down what is worth keeping and somewhere to read what an earlier run learned, with provenance attached so a human can see where a claim came from. It is being built at pilot scope, on the services the platform already runs.

Alongside the platform, Foundation-scale security scanning has continued. A recent pass covered 230 repositories across 75 project management committees in three days. The results of that work are what the memory pilot is being tested against first.

Two adjacent projects came up repeatedly in the hallway track as well: Apache Magpie, agent-assisted infrastructure for maintaining open source repositories, and Apache Sourcelume, instrumentation for tracking the provenance of AI training data.

Coming up: FeatherCast

We recorded with FeatherCast, the ASF's podcast, while we were in Glasgow. The episode is not out yet; we will link it here and on What's New when it lands.

Getting involved

The initiative does its work in public and the easiest way in is to show up on the list.

  • Mailing list: general@rai.apache.org
  • ASF Slack: #rai-discuss (ASF Member-only)
  • The gateway: llm.apache.org
  • More ways in: Get involved
